rfi_map.label: Rethinking primary care
rfi_map.asked: CMS asked: how should Medicare pay for continuous, team-based primary care instead of visit-by-visit?
rfi_map.why_wh: Menopause, midlife and preventive women's care are longitudinal, team-based medicine, exactly what visit-by-visit payment fails. Whatever model CMS builds here is the future home of that care.

decoder.d: a monthly payment for managing your ongoing care, instead of billing visit by visit
care that happens across months of check-ins and counseling, the kind quick-visit billing undercounts

consider: Menopause and midlife care are months of counseling, not a 15-minute visit, any new payment model should count that work.
Ask whether the monthly-payment model will include menopause management explicitly, or leave it priced as a quick visit.

asks.ask: Clarify third-party software licensing doesn't block remote care billing; preserve chronic-pain codes.
asks.org: I am a board-certified emergency physician and the founder and CEO of BellyMD, Inc., a company building software supporting the longitudinal diagnosis and management of disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI). In summary, the attached comment: (1) supports the intent of the proposed employed-clinical-staff requirement for RPM and RTM services, and requests that the final rule state explicitly that the requirement applies to the furnishing of clinical services and that licensing software, devices, or data infrastructure from a third party does not affect billing eligibility when employed clinical staff perform the clinical work; (2) responding to the primary care redesign solicitation, requests that CMS preserve and strengthen the chronic pain management codes G3002 and G3003 and clarify that algorithmically summarized, patient-generated longitudinal data can support the assessment, care-plan, and monitoring elements of care management services when reviewed and acted on by the billing clinician; and (3) encourages CMS to propose a Physician Fee Schedule analog to th

asks.ask: Preserve standard pay rate; use authority or ask Congress for permanent inflation-linked raises.
asks.org: Physician payment has failed to keep pace with the Medicare Economic Index & practice cost inflation for over 20yrs.Allowing a temporary statutory increase to lapse w/o any offsetting adjustment effectively imposes a real-terms pay cut on physicians for the 6th time in 7yrs.Unlike hospitals &other Medicare facilities, physician payment has no permanent inflation-based update mechanism.Practices cannot absorb repeated reductions w/o reducing staff, limiting Medicare patient panels, closing altogether or refusing participation in medicare outcomes that directly threaten beneficiary access to care, particularly in rural & underserved areas

asks.ask: Extend family caregiver emotional support via trained navigators.
Support coaching codes with certified trainers; allow nurse oversight instead of direct supervision.
Support clinical-trial guidance code and technology-enabled primary care with patient safeguards.

rfi_map.label: Who 'owns' a patient's care (ACOs)
rfi_map.asked: CMS asked: how should patients be attributed to specialists and ACOs, who counts as your doctor?
rfi_map.why_wh: For many women, the OB/GYN is the principal doctor. Attribution rules decide whether Medicare's payment models recognize that or route women's care through someone else.

decoder.d: an Accountable Care Organization, a network of doctors and hospitals Medicare pays as a team to manage your whole care
Medicare's method for deciding which doctor “counts” as yours, that doctor gets the credit, the data, and the payment incentives for your care

consider: For many women, the OB/GYN is the main doctor. If Medicare's rules don't recognize that, women's care gets credited to someone else.
Ask CMS to let an OB/GYN count as a woman's principal physician in these doctor networks.

asks.ask: Don't create two-tier network pay; incentivize complexity recognition through network structure.
asks.org: Physician payment has failed to keep pace with the Medicare Economic Index & practice cost inflation for over 20yrs.Allowing a temporary statutory increase to lapse w/o any offsetting adjustment effectively imposes a real-terms pay cut on physicians for the 6th time in 7yrs.Unlike hospitals &other Medicare facilities, physician payment has no permanent inflation-based update mechanism.Practices cannot absorb repeated reductions w/o reducing staff, limiting Medicare patient panels, closing altogether or refusing participation in medicare outcomes that directly threaten beneficiary access to care, particularly in rural & underserved areas

Clarify network and specialist attribution rules.
Clarify network and specialist attribution rules.
Extend nursing-home complexity pay bonus (modifier) to SNF patients in doctor networks.

rfi_map.label: The annual well-woman visit
rfi_map.asked: CMS asked: should the Annual Wellness Visit be redesigned, and what should a modern one include?
rfi_map.why_wh: The opening to build a real well-woman visit into Medicare, screening, menopause, bone and heart health in one covered visit. Almost nobody is answering this question.

decoder.d: the Annual Wellness Visit, the free yearly planning check-in Medicare covers (it is not a full physical)

consider: This is the opening to build a real well-woman visit into Medicare: menopause status, bone health, and heart risk as named components.
Almost nobody is answering this question, a handful of specific, evidence-backed answers could shape the visit for a generation.

asks.ask: Keep same-day annual wellness and chronic-care visits; 50% cut forces separate appointments, misses cancer screening.
Allow community clinics same-day annual wellness billing and nurse care like federally-qualified clinics.
Require annual wellness visit to include physical exam for full preventive care.
Allow community clinics same-day annual wellness billing and nurse care like federally-qualified clinics.
Redesign annual wellness to meet women's full preventive care needs.

rfi_map.label: Measuring care quality
rfi_map.asked: CMS asked: what should Medicare measure, and how should quality data flow?
rfi_map.why_wh: What isn't measured is invisible. No women's-health measures in MVPs means no accountability for menopause care, maternal outcomes, or screening rates.

decoder.d: a bundled scorecard of quality measures Medicare uses to grade specialists
a tracked statistic (screening rates, outcomes), in Medicare, what isn't measured is invisible

consider: There is no menopause-management measure on any Medicare scorecard. Propose one, what gets measured gets managed.
Ask for maternal-health and screening outcomes to be trackable in the data CMS is designing now.

asks.ask: Enable transparent data collection for quality tracking.
Include LDL-C outcome measure (LDL <70 mg/dL) in MIPS to address cardiovascular care gaps and disparities in women/minorities.
Use electronic quality measures for real-world function to reduce reporting burden.
Record AI oversight in billing record, not policy form; support monitoring and problem diagnosis.
Enable health record sharing for quality while maintaining AI ethics and validation standards.

rfi_map.label: How medical codes are set & priced
rfi_map.asked: CMS asked: how should we decide what a medical service is worth, and what evidence should count?
rfi_map.why_wh: This is where gynecologic undervaluation gets fixed: decades of research show female-coded procedures priced ~30% below male-coded equivalents. Evidence standards set here decide whether that record can move CMS.

decoder.d: the numbered catalog of every billable medical service, if it isn't in the catalog, it can't be paid for
a committee of physicians convened by the AMA that recommends what each service should pay; CMS historically accepts ~9 in 10 of its numbers
the “work units” behind every Medicare price

consider: Ask for a routine sex-based audit of prices: identical work should never pay less because the patient is a woman.
Name the missing codes: menopause management, endometriosis care by complexity, perimenopause, conditions the catalog can't see today.
Push for objective evidence, operating-room logs and registry time data, not self-reported surveys, because that's the evidence CMS says it acts on.

questions.label: Where has the coding process failed patient care?

samples.text: Undervalued gynecologic surgery reduces surgeon supply and access.
Inadequate codes for integrative care create barriers to patient access.
Complex endometriosis surgery is undervalued relative to its complexity.
Many non-drug services lack accurate codes and fit poorly into existing ones.

questions.label: What should replace or check the CPT/RUC process?

samples.text: Conduct a comprehensive sex-equity audit of current pay valuations.
Allow alternative billing codes to capture integrative services CPT omits.
Use objective, evidence-based methods for determining physician work values.
AI reducing documentation shouldn't reduce payment for physician work.

questions.label: Should services be grouped or bundled differently?

samples.text: Eliminate sex-specific codes where underlying surgical work is equivalent.
Separate and transparently show nursing labor and contributions in payment.

rows.org: As an emergency physician, I urge CMS to avoid implementing additional efficiency reductions to emergency department evaluation and management (E/M) or critical care services unless there is clear evidence that the physician work required to provide these services has actually decreased. Emergency physicians maintain continuous readiness to care for any patient at any time, including fulfilling EMTALA obligations, providing surge capacity during disasters and high-volume periods, caring for uninsured and underinsured patients, and managing the substantial workload created by prolonged emergency department boarding. These essential responsibilities generate significant costs that should be recognized in Medicare payment policy. CMS should also ensure that emergency physicians are not unfairly penalized under the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) for factors outside their control, such as inpatient bed shortages, consultant delays, psychiatric placement barriers, staffing shortages, and other hospital operational issues that prolong emergency department stays.
